text: India's AYUSH exports growing rapidly — USD 500+ million annually. Key markets: USA, EU, Middle East, Southeast Asia, Africa. Export products: Ayurvedic medicines, herbal supplements, cosmetics, raw herbs, extracts. Regulatory framework involves: CDSCO for drug classification, APEDA/PHARMEXCIL for export promotion, DGFT for licenses, Customs for clearances, and destination country regulations. For AYUSH exporters: understand both Indian export requirements AND target country import regulations.

Export licenses required: 1) IEC Code — Importer Exporter Code from DGFT (mandatory for all exporters). 2) AD Code — registration with authorized dealer bank. 3) RCMC — Registration Cum Membership Certificate from export promotion council (PHARMEXCIL for pharma/AYUSH). Additional for specific products: Drug Export License (Form 28D) for scheduled drugs, Phytosanitary certificate for plant materials, CITES permit for protected species. FSSAI registration if exporting as food products.

Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (CoPP) from CDSCO required by many importing countries. CoPP certifies: 1) Product is authorized for sale in India. 2) Manufacturing plant is licensed and inspected. 3) Product meets quality standards. Application: online through SUGAM portal. Fee: Rs 1,000. Processing: 15-30 days. Validity: 2 years. Alternative: Free Sale Certificate (FSC) for products not requiring drug approval. Many countries accept CoPP as evidence of product legitimacy.

WHO-GMP certification increasingly required for AYUSH exports, especially to regulated markets. WHO-GMP for AYUSH covers: premises, equipment, personnel, documentation, production, quality control, self-inspection. Certification process: 1) Apply to CDSCO/State FDA. 2) Document review. 3) Plant inspection. 4) Certificate issued if compliant. Validity: 3 years. Benefits: access to more markets, premium pricing, improved quality systems. Investment: facility upgrades, training, documentation systems.

Exporting AYUSH to USA: 1) Dietary supplements — regulated under DSHEA, need FDA facility registration, proper labeling with supplement facts panel, no disease claims. 2) Drugs — need FDA approval (NDA/ANDA), very expensive and time-consuming. 3) Cosmetics — FDA registration recommended, proper labeling, no drug claims. Most AYUSH products enter as dietary supplements or cosmetics. Warning: FDA strict on claims — 'treats diabetes' = drug, needs approval; 'supports healthy blood sugar' = supplement, allowed. Work with US regulatory consultant.

Exporting AYUSH to EU: 1) Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products (THMP) — simplified registration if 30 years use including 15 in EU. 2) Food supplements — must comply with Food Supplements Directive. 3) Novel foods — new ingredients need EFSA approval (lengthy process). 4) Cosmetics — comply with Cosmetics Regulation, safety assessment required. Challenge: many Ayurvedic herbs are 'novel' in EU (no traditional use history there). Strategy: enter as food supplement for established herbs, cosmetics for topical products. CE marking not required for supplements but helps.

Exporting AYUSH to Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC): 1) SFDA registration (Saudi), DHA/MOH registration (UAE), etc. required. 2) Arabic labeling mandatory in most countries. 3) Halal certification increasingly expected — no alcohol, no animal-derived ingredients (or halal-certified animals). 4) Product registration process: 3-6 months typically. 5) Authorized local distributor/agent often required. For AYUSH: avoid products with alcohol-based extraction, get Halal certification proactively, partner with established Middle East distributors.

Southeast Asian AYUSH export opportunities: 1) Many countries have traditional medicine frameworks accommodating Ayurveda. 2) ASEAN Harmonized Traditional Medicines Registration simplifying process. 3) Countries: Malaysia (NPRA registration), Singapore (HSA registration), Thailand (Thai FDA), Indonesia (BPOM). 4) Growing health-conscious middle class. 5) Cultural affinity with Indian traditional medicine. Challenges: local registration in each country, local language requirements, competition from local traditional medicines (TCM, Jamu).

Export documentation checklist: 1) Commercial invoice. 2) Packing list. 3) Bill of lading/airway bill. 4) Certificate of origin. 5) CoPP or Free Sale Certificate. 6) Certificate of Analysis. 7) WHO-GMP certificate (if required). 8) Phytosanitary certificate (for plant materials). 9) NBA approval if biological resource based. 10) Halal certificate (for Middle East). 11) CITES permit (if protected species). 12) Health certificate (some countries). Work with freight forwarders experienced in pharmaceutical/supplement exports.

Government export incentives for AYUSH: 1) RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products) — refund of embedded taxes. 2) Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) scheme — duty-free import of capital goods for export production. 3) Advance Authorization — duty-free import of inputs for exports. 4) Market Access Initiative (MAI) — support for market development. 5) Trade Infrastructure for Export Scheme (TIES). 6) PHARMEXCIL support programs. 7) AYUSH Export Promotion Council activities. Register and utilize available incentives to improve competitiveness.

Export labeling requirements vary by destination: 1) USA — Supplement Facts panel, ingredient list with botanical names, manufacturer/distributor info, net contents, 'Not evaluated by FDA' disclaimer. 2) EU — nutrition declaration, allergen info, batch number, best before date, origin country. 3) GCC — Arabic translation, Halal logo if applicable. 4) General — English labeling minimum, local language often required. Never make disease treatment claims on export labels. Country-specific compliance essential — incorrect labeling leads to customs rejection.

Heavy metal content is major export barrier for AYUSH products. Limits vary by country — EU and US have stringent standards. Common issues: 1) Lead, mercury, arsenic in herbal raw materials (soil contamination). 2) Bhasma/mineral preparations have inherent metal content. Solutions: 1) Source from tested, certified suppliers. 2) Test every batch before export. 3) Avoid products with unavoidable high metal content in strict markets. 4) Consider reformulating for export (remove problematic ingredients). 5) Certification of analysis from accredited labs builds buyer confidence.

Protect IP in export markets: 1) Trademark registration in target countries (Madrid Protocol helps). 2) Patent protection if applicable (PCT national phases). 3) Domain name registration for online sales. 4) Customs recordal in key markets to stop counterfeits. Risk: successful products get copied quickly; if you don't have IP protection in the target market, you have no recourse. Strategy: register IP in key markets before/alongside market entry. Budget IP as part of export expansion cost.

Indian AYUSH manufacturers can do contract manufacturing for foreign brands. Requirements: 1) WHO-GMP certification for the facility. 2) Proper quality agreements. 3) Export documentation under Indian company or in foreign company's name (toll manufacturing). 4) NBA approval if foreign company is accessing Indian biological resources. 5) Compliance with destination country requirements. Benefits: utilize excess capacity, guaranteed volumes, technology transfer opportunities. Risks: dependency, IP leakage, margin pressure.
